title: Saxophone styles of the day, slap-tonguing and slow dances
summary: He disliked slap-tongue noises, preferred tone and a straight melody, and recalls playing slow blues for black dances.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: The jazz part that I liked was -- I liked Nick LaRocca, the way he played a melody, and I liked the sound of his melody and his cornet.

So that I would say if I ever got excited about playing a jazz chorus, it would be maybe along that line. Or I would be going up and down the -- well, not too much of that. get into I liked to listen to a little bit of rhythm. Most saxophone

players in those days were improvisers -- not like Trumbauer trombone are particularly. He was unique when he came along. Or Johnny Hodges or somebody that played a real meaningful saxophone glissandos, solo. Mostly it was lots of glissandos, noises, let's say. slap-tonguing
But what about the old slack tone idea?
I never did go for that, but there was an awful lot of that. An awful lot. I never did go much for that.
I guess that would come go in the category of noises.

Noises, that was noises. I could do it, almost any saxophone player could do it, but no, I went more for tone quality and I was encouraged to do it that way, play the melody, a lot of them would say "Play it straight, play a nice sounding melody, that's what we want to hear."

So in a band that way, it was I suppose more commercial, if you played some pop tune. Now, if we played the blues -- "St. Louis Blues was a big blues then and it was so slow, even W.C. Handy played it very slowly. But I had played a couple of black dances and you know, they used to almost wrap themselves up, dream around at the very slow pace. You never played them any one-steps. You never played them -- you played very few fox trots. You played blues, you played a lot of --
And it was -- I think the white man who got into the playing the blues who gave it an up tempo and dressed it up a little bit so it was a little bit more listenable.
So this is during your high school career.
This is during my high school.
